opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's probably the most common misconception I run into, and it's a really reasonable one. If you write a piece of software, you understand it, right? You wrote every line. But language models are different, and the best analogy I've found is that we don't really build them so much as grow them.

What we actually write is pretty small. We write the architecture, which is a fairly simple recipe of repeated layers, and we write a training procedure that says, roughly, "here's a ton of text, get better at predicting the next word." Then we run that for an enormous amount of compute, and the training process adjusts billions of numbers to make the predictions better. Nobody sits there deciding what any of those numbers should be. So at the end you have this artifact that can write poetry, solve math problems, translate between languages, and the honest answer to "how does it do that?" is that we didn't put any of that in on purpose. It emerged.

It's a bit like biology. You can know the full genome of an organism and the rules of how cells divide, and still have no idea how the brain does what it does. Knowing the low-level rules doesn't give you the high-level mechanisms.

And that's what interpretability is trying to recover. We can see every single number in the model, which is actually a huge advantage over neuroscience, but those numbers are not organized in a way that's readable to us. So the work is building tools, kind of like a microscope, to look inside and ask: when the model answers this question, what intermediate concepts is it representing? Is it actually planning ahead? Is it doing the math the way it says it is, or is it doing something else and then telling a plausible story afterward?

Some of the things we've found are genuinely surprising. For example, when a model writes a rhyming poem, you might assume it's just going word by word, but you can see it picking the rhyme word in advance and then writing the line to land there. Or when you ask it how it added two numbers, it'll describe the carry-the-one algorithm from school, but internally it's doing something quite different, with parallel paths estimating the rough magnitude and the exact last digit. The model's explanation of itself and what it's actually doing don't always match.

That's exactly why this matters. As these systems get deployed in more consequential settings, "it seems to work on the tests we tried" isn't a great foundation. We want to be able to say why a model gave an answer, whether it's reasoning faithfully, whether there's some hidden behavior we haven't triggered yet. And you can't get that just from having built it. You have to go in and actually study it, almost like a natural scientist studying something that was handed to them.

r001.rationale: The response says that building and training a model does not reveal how it produces its behavior: its capabilities emerge from training, and knowing the low-level recipe does not explain the high-level mechanisms.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that's counterintuitive is that there's a difference between building something and understanding it, and with language models that gap is unusually large. The analogy I like is that we didn't really build the model in the way you build a bridge, where you design every beam and you know why it's there. What we built is the training process. We set up the architecture, we set up the data, we set up the objective, and then we ran an optimization for a very long time, and the thing that came out the other end has hundreds of billions of parameters that nobody wrote. Nobody sat down and said this weight should be 0.3. So in a sense it's closer to growing something than engineering it, and if you grow a plant you don't automatically know how photosynthesis works just because you planted the seed.

And I think the way this hits people is when you ask very simple questions. Why did the model say this? Why did it refuse that? Why does it sometimes make up a citation that looks plausible? Why does it get a math problem right one way and wrong when you rephrase it? The honest answer from the people who trained it is often, we don't know, we can speculate, we can run some evals, but we can't actually look inside and point to the mechanism. And that would be a pretty strange situation for any other piece of software. If your database did something surprising, you'd open the code and trace it. Here you can open it up and all you see is a giant pile of numbers.

So interpretability is really the attempt to close that gap, to go from the pile of numbers to something like concepts and algorithms, so that when the model does something we can say, okay, here's the feature that represents this idea, here's how it got activated, here's how it influenced the output. And I think that matters for a few reasons. One is just scientific curiosity, these are the most complex artifacts we've ever made and it's a little embarrassing not to understand them. But the more practical reason is that these systems are getting deployed in places where the stakes are real, and if you want to trust them, or debug them, or make sure they're not doing something you didn't intend, you need more than just observing behavior from the outside. Behavior tells you what happened on the inputs you tried. Understanding the mechanism is what lets you say something about the inputs you didn't try.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly distinguishes building a language model from understanding it, explaining that training produces many parameters nobody designed and that its behavioral mechanisms are often unknown.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is that we understand how we train these models, but that doesn’t mean we understand the solution they learn. We design the architecture, we choose the training objective, and we build the process that updates the weights. But we don’t write down the algorithm the model ultimately uses to answer a question. That algorithm emerges through training.

So you can know exactly how every individual operation works and still not have a useful explanation for why the model gave a particular answer. You can test it on lots of examples, and that tells you a lot about its behavior. But if it succeeds, was it using the reasoning you hoped it would use, or was it relying on some shortcut that won’t hold up in a different setting?

That’s the motivation for interpretability: to look inside the model and try to understand the mechanisms producing its behavior. Building the system gives us access to its internals. Understanding those internals is a separate research problem.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes knowing how the model is built and trained from understanding the learned algorithm or mechanisms that produce its answers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction is between understanding how we train a model and understanding the particular solution that training produces. We know the architecture, we know the objective, and we know how we update the weights. But we don’t write down the algorithm the model ultimately uses to answer a question. That algorithm is learned, and it’s represented across billions of parameters.

So if you ask, “Why did it give this answer?” we can describe the training process, but that doesn’t necessarily explain what happened inside the model in that instance. And asking the model to explain itself doesn’t resolve that, because its explanation is another output—it isn’t a direct readout of its internal computation.

Interpretability research is about closing that gap. Can we identify what the model represents, how it uses those representations, and test those explanations by intervening on the model? The goal is to move from observing behavior to understanding enough of the mechanism that we can better predict when it will work and when it might fail.

r001.rationale: The candidate distinguishes knowing the model’s architecture, objective, and training updates from knowing the learned algorithm it uses to answer questions, explaining that building it does not reveal the mechanisms behind its behavior.
